sentences.text: 2025:KER:19417  JUDGMENT Dated this the 06th day of March, 2025 This Land Acquisition Appeal is filed by the State challenging the judgment dated 19.01.2012 in L.A.R.No.33 of 2006 of the Subordinate Judge's Court, Thiruvalla.

Respondents were the claimants in the L.A.R.
2.

An extent of 1.45 Ares of land comprised in Sy.No.498/11 and an extent of 6.90 Ares of land in Sy.No.499/13 in Block No.5 of Nedumpuram Village, Thiruvalla Taluk, was acquired for the purpose of construction of the Madanaserri Kadavu bridge.
The notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was published on 05.12.2003.
The Land Acquisition Officer (L.A.O.) awarded land value at the rate of Rs.18,560/- per Are.
In the reference that followed, the reference court refixed the land value at Rs.30,000/- per cent.
The State had preferred L.A.A.No.1531 of 2009 wherein this Court had remanded the matter back for fresh consideration.
After such remand, the reference court had re-fixed 2025:KER:19417 the land value at Rs.50,000/- per Are.
An amount of Rs.50,000/- was also granted towards injurious affection.
Challenging the same, this appeal has been filed by the State.
3. Heard Smt.Rekha C.Nair, learned Senior Government Pleader for the appellants.
Though service of notice was completed on the respondents, there was no appearance on their behalf.
4. The learned Senior Government Pleader submitted that the reference court erred in refixing the land value at Rs.50,000/- per Are.
The court after rightly rejecting Exts.A1 and A2 sale deeds went to refix the land value at the rate of Rs.50,000/- without any basis.
The land value fixed by the L.A.O. was just and reasonable.

The amount of Rs.50,000/- awarded towards injurious affection is State Of Kerala, Rep.By District ... vs Saramma Thomas & Ors on 6 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167606235/
2 without any evidence as to how much of the land remains after the acquisition as well as the percentage of injury or diminution if any caused to the remaining land.

entities.text: State Of Kerala, Rep.By District ... vs Saramma Thomas & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Though a Commission was taken out, the measurement of property for ascertaining the damage, if any, caused to the remaining land was never undertaken.
It was thus submitted that the appeal may be allowed and the land value fixed 2025:KER:19417 by the L.A.O. may be affirmed.
5. The respondents/claimants relied on Exts.A1 and A2 sale deeds to assert their claim for enhancement.
AW1 to AW4 were examined.
Commission reports and rough sketches [C1, C1 (a), C2 and C2 (a)] were relied on.
Ext.A1 is a sale deed dated 15.05.2006 and Ext.A2 is a sale deed dated 18.02.2005.
Section 4(1) notification was published on 05.12.2003.
Thus, both the said sale deeds are post-notification documents.
They were hence found by the reference court to be unreliable for assessing the market value.

Ext.R3 sale deed dated 28.12.2001 produced by the respondents was also found to be an unreliable document to fix the land value inter alia for the reason that the properties were situated in different villages.

Taking note of the Commission report which mentioned that the acquired property had access to PWD road the reference court held that the land value of Rs.18,560/- per Are fixed by the L.A.O. cannot be termed just and reasonable.

Thereafter relying on the Commission reports and the sketches, which revealed that the property is situated in an important area which could be termed as a 2025:KER:19417 residential area and that it has road access with some important institutions in the vicinity, it was concluded that the same would fetch at least Rs.50,000/- per Are at the time of 4 (1) notification ie., on 05.12.2003.
It was thus found that the claimants are entitled to receive an enhanced land value of Rs.31,440/- per Are after deducting the land value of Rs.18,560/- per Are already awarded by the L.A.O.

Since it was revealed in evidence that due to the acquisition, the property had been divided into two segments thereby diminishing its width and rendering it unfit for any construction purpose or even for the construction of a residential building therein, the reference court had found that the claimants are entitled to compensation for severance.
An amount of Rs.50,000/- was thus awarded towards compensation for severance.

6. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has in New Okhla Industrial Development Authority v. Harnand Singh (Deceased) through LRs and others [(2024) SCC OnLine SC 1691] considered the applicability and use of the principle of 'guesstimation' and has held that "32.

entities.text: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority v. Harnand Singh (Deceased) through LRs and others [(2024) SCC OnLine SC 1691]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This principle accentuates the fundamental 2025:KER:19417 understanding that determining compensation for land is not a matter of exact science but involves a significant element of estimation.

Indeed, this holds true for valuation of land in general, which is affected by a multitude of factors such as its location,
surrounding market conditions, feasible uses etc.
Accordingly, while evidence and calculations can aid in estimating the land value, they ultimately serve as tools for approximation rather than precision.

Instead, land valuation--and consequently the affixation of compensation remains an exercise of informed estimation, requiring the integration of diverse data points and professional judgment concerning subjective, intangible and dynamic elements.
Pursuing a single precise valuation or compensation figure is bound to be unjust, representing a rigid approach and a procrustean endeavour at best.
33. Having said that, it is important to clarify that the process of determining compensation is not entirely subjective.

While it may not be possible to arrive at a definitive figure, the exercise is still State Of Kerala, Rep.By District ... vs Saramma Thomas & Ors on 6 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167606235/
3 epistemologically objective in so far as it is grounded in evidence and the consideration of relevant factors.

entities.text: State Of Kerala, Rep.By District ... vs Saramma Thomas & Ors on 6 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In case the compensation is fixed agnostically to the factors affecting the valuation of the land, the resultant figure might be arbitrary and may fail to adequately compensate the landowner for the expropriated land.
Hence, while some subjectivity may exist in fixing the final figure based on these factors, the sliding scale of judicial discretion cannot be extended to mere speculation.
34. Accordingly, while the Court can use the principle of guesstimation in reasonably estimating the value of land in the absence of direct evidence, the exercise ought not to be purely hypothetical.

Instead, the Court must embrace a holistic view and consider all relevant factors and existing evidence, even if not directly comparable, to arrive at a fair determination of compensation."
(Emphasis added)

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has thus laid down the three categories 2025:KER:19417 of relevant factors that ought to be considered while determining the estimated value of the land to determine a fair amount of compensation in land acquisition proceedings.

The same are as follows:
"i. Characteristics of the land: The valuation of land is undeniably influenced by its inherent characteristics.

A parcel of land endowed with advantageous features that enhance its accessibility and usability tends to command higher market price and thus, a greater valuation in comparison to lands lacking such attributes.

Key factors contributing to such features include connectivity via roads and other means of transportation, the size and shape of the land, availability of essential utilities such as electricity and water, the evenness or levelling of the land's surface, width of frontage,
and nature and status of the surrounding area etc. ii.
Future potentiality of the land:
In addition to its characteristics, the valuation of land is also influenced by its potentiality.

Lands with the potential to be used for commercial or residential purposes; that are located in or near a developed area; or which are proximate to tourist destinations, are perceived to hold greater value in the future.

Consequently,
landowners may anticipate higher future prices and accordingly demand higher sale prices compared to lands lacking these attributes.
Accordingly, these features also lead to an increase in valuation; and iii. Factors denoting market sentiment: Market sentiments are powerful drivers of land valuation.

Even if a particular piece of land possesses all desirable features, its valuation can still suffer if the market conditions at the time of publication of the notification under Section 4 of the 1894 Act were unfavourable.
Factors such as economic recessions, political instability, speculative investments or real estate crisis can impact the perceived value of the land.

Thus,
these 2025:KER:19417 extraneous economic and political factors must also be considered when assessing land valuation."
(Emphasis added)
7. Bearing in mind the above mandate as laid down by the Supreme Court, I have examined the detailed reasoning given by the reference court after appreciating the evidence put forth by both sides.

It is noted that the learned Judge has exhaustively considered the documents produced,
including the Commission report, and had arrived at the land value per Are at Rs.50,000/- during State Of Kerala, Rep.
By District

... vs Saramma Thomas & Ors on 6 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167606235/
4 the relevant time, viz., that of 4 (1) notification, which is dated 05.12.2003.

I note that the learned Sub Judge had taken into consideration the importance of the locality, road access, presence of other institutions in the vicinity etc. as relevant aspects as discernible from the Commission report and other records produced in evidence.

That due to the acquisition, the property of the claimants had been divided into two segments thereby diminishing its width and rendering it unfit for the construction of a residential or commercial building had also been factored in.

On the whole, the course adopted by the learned Judge in endeavouring a 'guesstimation' and 2025:KER:19417 in refixing the land value @Rs.50,000/- per Are and the award of Rs.50,000/- towards injurious affection cannot be termed as unreasonable or illegal.
I do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment dated 19.01.2012 in L.A.R.No.33 of 2006 of the Subordinate Judge's Court, Thiruvalla.
This Appeal is dismissed.
